replying_to: Replying to Regularization for Strategy Exploration in Empirical Game-Theoretic Analysis
display_title: Official Review of Paper1475 by Reviewer mVn8

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces Regularized Replicator Dynamics (RRD), which the authors claim can practically outperform exact Nash and other related methods as the meta-strategy solver in PSRO.
content.main_review:
Strengths

1. RRD is simple to implement and explain
2. The techniques in the paper are extremely general and can basically be applied to any game verbatim

Major questions/concerns

1. Why replicator dynamics, as opposed to any other iterative method with perhaps more theoretical guarantees (such as no-regret learning, or linear programming)? If the "stability" of the method (i.e., meta-profiles not changing much between PSRO iterations) is the key (as suggested in the experiments section), it seems to me that any iterative method that can be warm-started (e.g., regret matching) can lead to this as well, or it can be added as an explicit objective to a linear program. These would perhaps be more preferable, as, unlike RD, they are guaranteed to find Nash (at least in zero-sum games). I would like to see at least a deeper/more mathematically rigorous discussion about such alternatives, both theoretically and practically, to tease out exactly what it is about the MSS that gives good convergence.

1. In the description of BPS, what, exactly, is a subgame? There are two possibilities in my mind:

(a) *A subgame is an empirical game.* That is, a subgame of an empirical game is a tuple of collection of strategies in the empirical game, one collection per player. If this is the interpretation, the number of payoff matrix entries that need to be computed still scales poorly with the number of players: if we have lots of players each with 2 strategies {L, R}, then BPS will start with 1 strategy for each player (say L), and at each iteration (until convergence) will add strategy R for a new player. Thus after $t$ iterations of BPS our subgame will have 2 strategies for each of $t$ players and 1 strategy for each of the remainder, for a total of $2^t$ profiles. Is the hope that the number of iterations required for convergence will be so tiny that $2^t$ is controlled? That seems unlikely to me. Indeed, in the experiments (Table 1), using BPS does not have a large impact on the number of iterations, only about 10% decrease.

(b) *A subgame is a collection of profiles*. If this is the interpretation, we still run into trouble: a collection of strategy profiles may not make a game. For example, if two players each have two strategies {L, R}, the collection of profiles {LL, LR, RR} do not form a game. What, then, does it mean to compute a Nash equilibrium in a subgame?

3. A lot of the experiments have large relatively error bars that make the results not significant or only slightly significant. I would like to see a more rigorous test with more games and more samples, if the main claims of the paper are to be empirical.

1. The construction in the proof of Theorem 2 ("No free lunch") is circular: the game $\mathcal G$ depends on the strategies $s_t$ and $s'_t$, which depend on the sequences $\{X_t\}$ and $\{X'_t\}$ of empirical games, which depend on the game $\mathcal G$. 

Minor questions/comments

5. Theorem 1 explicitly relies on RRS converging to a $\lambda$-equilibrium, which may not happen. This should be explicitly stated as a condition. 

1. In the experiments, what size board is used for Hex, and how is the regret computed? I assume a very small one, as it is easily solved by these techniques and regret is exactly computable.
content.summary_of_the_review: Paper's main claims are not very well justified: why RRS and BPS as opposed to several reasonable alternatives?
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Thanks for all the comments and suggestions.
content.comment:
The purpose of RD is to search towards a NE in the empirical game stopping if the regret threshold is satisfied. Our key claim is that not best responding to an exact NE (i.e. regularization) would boost the learning performance. We are open to alternative solvers implementing the idea of regularization (i.e., not best responding to the exact NE). But the effectiveness of these solvers should be verified through experiments. 

As stated in the “No Free Lunch Theorem”, no MSS can dominate all other MSSs in any game. Therefore, proving one is better than another in terms of convergence is impossible in the PSRO framework. 

For BPS, a subgame of an empirical game is a tuple of collection of strategies in the empirical game. It is a subgame of the empirical game. In extreme situations like the one mentioned by the reviewer, BPS would be less effective since the dimension of the payoff matrix expands largely according to the number of players. But this is not typical in games of interest.

The scale of the error bar is mainly caused by the nature of the game (e.g., games with high randomness). Similar observations have been made in previous studies.

In the proof of “NFL”, we are trying to construct a G such that m’ converges first. We can always construct a game such that the sequences X and X’ are the same by designing the payoff structure. When at certain iteration X and X’ differ, we can always make the profile they differ in X’ a NE , for example, by assigning large payoffs for all players to that profile. G is fixed for the strategy exploration but the order of whether m or m’ first finds the NE is manipulated. 

For Hex, we use the payoff table given by the paper Real-world games look like a spinning top. The size of the board is 3. We compute the regret with respect to the payoff table.

>  Our key claim is that not best responding to an exact NE (i.e. regularization) would boost the learning performance. We are open to alternative solvers implementing the idea of regularization (i.e., not best responding to the exact NE). But the effectiveness of these solvers should be verified through experiments.

As this paper is mostly experimental and the key claim is rather counterintuitive, I would like to see these experiments with additional solvers. It is important, in my opinion, to get to the bottom of what is driving this result. RRD in particular, in my opinion, does not seem like it should be the "right" method, because, as the authors admit, it is not guaranteed to converge to a NE of the empirical game, and therefore PSRO+RRD does not necessarily converge to NE. At the very least, I would recommend trying iterative algorithms such as regret minimization with early stopping, as that seems like a more natural means of regularization. Such rigorous experiments would greatly strengthen the main claims of the paper.

> In the proof of “NFL”, we are trying to construct a G such that m’ converges first. We can always construct a game such that the sequences X and X’ are the same by designing the payoff structure. When at certain iteration X and X’ differ, we can always make the profile they differ in X’ a NE , for example, by assigning large payoffs for all players to that profile. G is fixed for the strategy exploration but the order of whether m or m’ first finds the NE is manipulated.

That doesn't address my concern. With fixed MSSs, the game G determines the sequences X, X' of empirical games. So, you cannot construct a game G based on the sequences X, X'--that is circular. 

Perhaps I am just confused. In any case, it would help greatly to see the explicit construction of the counterexample game G and MSS m', rather than just "we can always do this".

replying_to: Replying to Response

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
Thank you for the suggestion. Regret minimization with early stopping is an alternative to implement the regularization in PSRO. As for the concerns on the performance of RRD, despite algorithms like DO guarantee a convergence to NE, it is possible that such algorithms need to explore a large number of strategies to reach the convergence in large games, which is far beyond the computational budget. Therefore, for strategy exploration, we hope to design new MSSs that are able to fast decrease the regret (i.e., learning stable profiles) within the computational budget. Although RRD has weaker convergence guarantee in the limit, it is able to learn stable profiles quickly within the budget by controlling the degree of regularization. This fulfills the goal of strategy exploration.

For the concern about the cyclic proof, the trick is that we can make the strategies where X and X' differ have no effect on the construction of X and X' before the difference. So in this case G is still fixed. We understand this could be abstract and will add more explanations and one example in the future.

content.title: subgames in BPS
content.comment: This comment directly addresses the query about subgames and skepticism about BPS. As the first author comment states, subgames in this context are simply games over strategy subsets. As the reviewer notes, this does not save us from exponential growth. Normal-form game representations (even with symmetry) are inherently exponential in the smaller of #players and #strategies. Requiring estimation of the full-game under PSRO, this can make it infeasible to go many iterations even with only 3 or 4 players, or even moderate numbers of iterations with 5 or more players. BPS lets us explore small-support subgames, which can dramatically extend the number of iterations we can go practically with moderate (say 3-8) numbers of players. (Theory tells us we can generally find approximate equilibria with support logarithmic in #strategies.) To deal with larger numbers of players, we would have to resort to other EGTA techniques like player reduction or game model regression.

content.comment:
I remain unconvinced of the utility of BPS. The experiments show that the gain from using BPS is only about 10% in all games. That isn't much.

In my original review, I remarked on the exponential dependence on the number of players because the paper explicitly discusses, when introducing BPS, the exponential dependence of empirical game sizes on the number of players. This suggests to the reader that the BPS will do something to address this weakness. But BPS does not address it. I therefore think the discussion about the exponential dependence should be removed, as it is not relevant and merely increases confusion.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
The BPS is presented in the context of PSRO. The extreme example given by the reviewer is not common in the applications of PSRO (including all related work) where PSRO develops a reasonable number of strategies for each player. The purpose of BPS is to mitigate the effect of growing number of players rather than solving it. 

Designing extreme cases against common game learning algorithms is cheap. For example, one can easily design a game to make DO enumerate all the strategies and converge slow than any other algorithms. (This is also indicated by the No Free Lunch Theorem in our paper.) However, those extreme cases are not the main concerns of common game learning algorithms.

For the utility of BPS, BPS essentially brings in a negligible computational burden compared to evaluating a profile. Moreover, BPS is easy to implement. For a PSRO practitioner, there is no reason to decline a nearly free 10% savings but insist on simulating the whole payoff matrix.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Policy-Space Response Oracle (PSRO) is an algorithm that incrementally approximates Nash Equilibria (NE) in an *original* game by maintaining a portfolio of strategies for all players, over which the final player strategies (the NE) must mix appropriately. PSRO updates the portfolio by employing Double Oracle (DO)-like iterations on an *empirical* game. There are two steps in this process: 1) The individual rewards of the empirical normal-form game are estimated by averaging simulations of the original game using each tuple of pure strategies from the portfolio. Then, 2) new strategies are added to expand the portfolio. They are found using reinforcement learning as an (approximate) best-response to some probability distribution over the opponent's profile. How to set this distribution is important: it will be used as a training target for RL.

Previously, the distribution (hence training target) was set as the NE of the opponents (with some minor modifications to incentivize exploration). This paper instead proposes to i) use an approximate NE as the target: it is found by following a few steps of replicator dynamics until a stopping criterion (regret or number of iterations) is met. Then ii), for a game with more than two players, authors provide a Double-Oracle-like scheme to select which rewards should be computed by simulation to save time, as the number of all non-sparse individual rewards to estimate is exponential in the number of players.
content.main_review:
The paper is relatively clearly written for an expert in the topic, but is perhaps less accessible for an outsider. A few more iterations on the text could improve clarity, for example simplifying the text of abstract to not use abbreviations unncessarily and improving the flow of the text.

This is mainly an experimental paper. My main concerns are following:

i) The main takeaway from the paper is that picking the opponent portfolio distribution as an approximate NE yields lower regret than an exact NE (for example, Figure 1b). I find this very surprising, and I suspect there are some confounding factors going on that deserve more thorough investigation and explanation. I suspect this is due to inexact values of the empirical game. The set of NE in the empirical game can be **very sensitive** to the choice of rewards, and perhaps some strategies dominate others due to variance of the simulated rewards. This effect might be even more pronounced, when old estimates are kept for the next iterations (such as in the OpenSpiel implementation of PSRO [1]). While this saves the time to recalculate the payoffs from O(n^2) to O(n), it could bias the search in the solution space and require more of pretty much identical DO strategies to compensate for the reward variance. 
As this shouldn't take too much time, I would like to ask the authors to rerun the experiments with exact rewards on the small games and show whether the observations in the paper still hold. Either way, this does not invalidate the findings on _large games_: it is prohibitively expensive to compute the rewards of the emprical game. But maybe more efficient mechanisms could be made (such as simulating more outcomes for the older strategies in the portfolio).

ii) How do the results generalize? The evaluations are run only on one sequential imperfect-information game (Leduc). It is not clear whether the additional complexity of having more hyperparameters to tune is worth it. Indeed, authors acknowledge this in the appendix as there is "No Free Lunch for the exploration strategies". For a practioner the results do not seem to be convincing enough to justify the additional cost.

iii) Why should one pick to use RD? I believe other alternatives could be used as well, such as parameter-free Regret Matching with convergence guarantees as a function of time, and are perhaps more efficient in this scenario.

iv) I'd like to suggest that the profile search in multiplayer (3+) games is out of scope of the paper and should be perhaps made into a separate publication. I understand the authors probably wanted to put as many interesting things in a single paper, but now there are "too many things going on" to properly analyze and review.

Other notes:

- "Our MSS exhibits many desired proprieties for strategy exploration" -- too vague, unclear what are "desired properties".
- PRD pseudocode: \sigma_i -- missing i 
- derivative of strategies -- please add reference to prev equation (with number).
- "a projection operator that maintains the feasibility of mixed strategies," -- a projection to strategy simplex
- "Since RD may not converge to an equilibrium in certain games" -- Note which games (or provide reference)
- "To handle this issue, we select by first running RD for a sufficient large number of iterations T' to obtain \lambda_\min and only choosing \lambda \geq \lambda_\min" -- how is this different to running RD for \tau iterations \tau < T' ? It seems like a roundabout way to claim that RRD will have some bounded regret. Couldn't the regret be directly computed from RD bounds?
- Everything is defined on NFG games, but Leduc Poker was evaluated -- did you turn the EFG to normal-form? (If yes, this is exponentially expensive and should be noted -- especially the RRD!). If not, then the algorithms are not properly defined.
- What is the cost of RRD compared to finding NE with LPs?
- Geometry of strategy space assembles the shape of a spinning top -- missing reference
- "plot the regret of RRD profile and the regret of NE based on the same empirical games in each run" -- in the whole game, not the "empirical game" right? because in empirical game NE regret would be zero (since it's the NE of that empirical game)
- Figure 5: what game is this? How robust are the results to selection with lambda? Does it hold generally across games? Is it an artefact of having imprecise values in the emprical game?
- Make very clear when regret is being measured on which game it is -- Figure 7? Unclear. 
- Observation: "Spikiness" may be related to the projection
- Sanity check: Are the regrets identical in iteration 1? Show full figures without truncation.
- "We evaluate MSSs in terms of the regret of MRCP (averaged over 5 different initial strategies for hex and starting from the uniform strategy for RGS), which is theoretically justified evaluation metric for PSRO when its computation is feasible" -- I don't see why this is justified.

[1] https://github.com/deepmind/open_spiel/blob/93c2ebd9479389aff3a00be1c83ff70615f357e9/open_spiel/python/algorithms/psro_v2/psro_v2.py#L398

[2] Grandmaster level in StarCraft II using multi-agent reinforcement learning, Vinyals et al.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes to study an interesting modification of PSRO and shows improvements in its regret performance. I like the idea of the paper, however I think the paper needs one more iteration. The authors should improve clarity, make more consise explanation of why approximate NE are better than the exact NE in the empirical game, evaluate on more imperfect-information games (as these are the main use-case for PSRO), and perhaps study alternative choices for finding the approximate NE.

content.title: Thanks for all the comments and detailed suggestions in the notes.
content.comment:
It is not surprising that there exists MSSs that outperform DO and the design of such MSSs is the goal of strategy exploration. For the payoff matrix evaluation, for the payoff of each profile in the empirical game, we run a sufficient number of episodes and take the averaged payoff. Moreover, since the evaluation of different profiles is independent from each other, payoff information from previous iterations remains effective for the latter iterations of PSRO. For details of our experiments, there is no sign of dominant strategies largely because the game is not transitive. We also tested our algorithm in matrix games with exact rewards and found DO is still not the best. 

There is no doubt that solving games like StarCraft II need more complex neural networks and extra tuning efforts than solving Leduc poker. Our algorithm does not introduce extra burden on the hyerparameter tuning besides the regret threshold lambda. To verify the performance of our algorithms, we consider multiple environments and 2-3-player games. 

We are open to alternative solvers implementing the idea of regularization (i.e., not best responding to the exact NE). But the effectiveness of these solvers should be verified through additional experiments.

Other notes:

The key point here is to acknowledge that RD will not generally converge to a NE, thus the existence of lambda_min. In the implementation, we pre-define a regret threshold lambda and run the RD. If the lambda is reached, we don’t need to figure out the lambda_min. Otherwise, we know lambda_min automatically (since RD has been running for a large number of iterations) and therefore adjust the regret threshold.

We treat the game as a black-box simulator and learn a NFG representation of it without knowing the exact structure of the EFG. This is a basic feature of learning with EGTA/PSRO.

Both RD and LP would not result in a computational burden to PSRO. The costly parts of PSRO are profile evaluation and the computation of best responses.

Yes, w.r.t the whole game.

Fig.5 and Fig.7 are based on 2-player Leduc poker. The stability of performance w.r.t lambda is shown in Fig.4(a), which indicates that there is a wide range of lambdas that yield better performance than DO. In the games we considered, the performance of our algorithm is stable with regularization. The payoffs in the empirical games are estimated through samples since we have no access to the exact utility function (i.e., we treat the game as a black-box simulator).

We define the empirical game in the first iteration of PSRO as the one after one best response operation. So in the first iteration, the regrets of target profiles are not the same even with the same initial strategy (i.e., uniform in our case). 

The performance of MRCP was justified by Wang et al. 2021. Not a part of this paper.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1475 by Reviewer BqzJ

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a variant of the PSRO family of double oracle algorithms, using replicator dynamics (RD) with strategy-profile regret to generate the next empirical game strategy to best-respond to, rather than the classic choice of trying to find a Nash equilibrium.  The RD process is terminated by reaching a threshold regret. The authors report on experiments showing this process has better performance in a couple of existing baselines, that using a regret-based stopping condition is better than a fixed number of update steps, and that the algorithm is not highly sensitive to the stopping threshold.
content.main_review:
The work in this paper is an interesting continuation of an existing strand of research. The algorithm is clear, but I have some concern about the applicability of theoretical statements, and the strength of the empirical results.

Finally, it wasn't clear to me what importance was being placed on solving two-player zero sum games, generating a strategically interesting set of strategies, and finding a NE (or some other eq'm concept?) for multiplayer games. As a result, the main text seems to largely be motivated and described in a multiplayer context, while the experiments seemed to be focused on two player zero-sum games. The results and much of the setup is centered around finding a strategy which is close to a NE, but there are occasional mentions of strategic diversity. The goal should be clear throughout the paper.


More specific comments follow below:

page 5: is lambda_min generated for each game? That is, every time we call RRD, do we run for many iterations to discover what lambda_min is, then either use a stored history or re-run to get the result for some larger lambda?
One issue I see is that if lambda_min is generated once early on, I'm not aware of any reason that cycles couldn't be introduced as the game is expanded, so that lambda_min might increase. If it's generated every time, how expensive is this?

Also related to lambda_min -- it's apparently part of the whole generation process, but its computation isn't well specified. Run once, or when? If once, with what initial empirical game (1 strategy doesn't seem like it would give an informative choice)? For what "large number of iterations"?

"Since RD may not converge to an equilibrium in certain games"
This seems like a weaker caveat than expected: in my understanding, RD is not guaranteed to converge in two player zero sum games (at least without adding additional regularization), let alone multiplayer games. An alternative phrasing like "Since RD will generally not converge to an equilibrium"?

Projection P seems to be defined wrt a generic norm. Did the authors intend this to be generic, or assuming some particular projection? If it is supposed to be a specific choice, that choice should be clarified. If P is intended to be generic, the choice used for the experiments should be stated.

Theorem 1 does not seem to directly apply to PSRO RRD.  Steps in the reasoning use a best response, while PSRO is using an approximate best response. Also, the set of all policies generated by the an RL-based approximate best-response oracle policies is only finite in an unsatisfying way: possible floating bit configurations of NN parameters, or some argument about the possible results given random data and a limited number of training step.
Ignoring the finite closure, it seems like it should be easy to update from a best response to an approximate best response.

The name epsilon-closeness suggests to me that epsilon is a parameter of the property, but it is instead a property of the argument, sigma. Also, closeness suggests a distance to me, rather than the propety of being closed. Consider calling it o-closed instead?

"We first observe that RRD yields a rapid convergence to a low-regret value compared to others."
Rephrase to be more clear that this is a relative to the other methods? The absolute values seem quite high, which is possibly being masked by the choice of clipping the y-axis: Leduc poker has a 1 unit ante, so a regret of 1 seems like rather a lot of regret. This is even more strongly an issue in Figure 3, which looks like minimal improvement over the initial (random?) strategy profile.

"According to the consistency criterion, we compare MSSs with the same RRD-based regret"
This could be clarified in the text. Figure 1b seems to have a number of different regret measurements, not just RRD. In contrast, Figure 1a is using a single measure: regret.

"and authenticate the faster convergence of RRD over DO and PRD in terms of the strategic coverage of the empirical game."
How is this a measure of strategic coverage? In what way is this critical?


Nit: for Figure 1a, suggest ordering the legend in the same order as the lines, by swapping RRD with threshold and RRD with fixed number of iterations. For Figure 2, use the same colors/legend for both plots.

content.title: Thanks for all the comments and suggestions.
content.comment:
The goal of EGTA is finding the NE of a game, which is also the goal of this paper. The strategic coverage measured by the metric proposed by Wang et al. 2021 means that in the profile space given by an empirical game, which profile is closest to the NE in terms of regret. So both Fig.1(a) and 1(b) measure the “distance” to the NE of the true game but evaluate the learning procedure from different angles (i.e., the regret of the profiles given by the corresponding MSSs (as in previous PSRO papers) and the quality of the profile spaces they create). 

For specific comments:

The motivation for having lambda_min is to remind people of the fact that RD will not generally converge to an exact NE. In the implementation, we pre-define a regret threshold lambda and run the RD. If the lambda is reached, we don’t need to figure out the lambda_min. Otherwise, we know lambda_min automatically (since RD has been running for a large number of iterations) and therefore adjust the regret threshold. All of our experiments on 2-player games fall into the first scenario and a very tiny number of iterations of the 3-player game meets the second case. So there is nearly no extra cost for finding lambda_min.

Thanks for all suggestions on paper expressions. 

We keep the norm generic in the paper since we found that both L-2 norm projection and lazy projection (simply normalizing) work for our algorithms. 

Theorem 1 assumes the exact best response oracle since the approximate best response may not find the optimal policy. The approximate best response would compromise the theoretical guarantee of PSRO with any MSS.

The regret mainly depends on the players’ strategies and less on the amount of ante. We focus on the overall learning performance and appreciate algorithms that exhibit good average performance.

Both Fig.1(a) and 1(b) measure the “distance” to the NE (i.e., regret) of the true game but evaluate the learning procedure from different angles (i.e., the regret of the profiles given by the corresponding MSSs (as in previous PSRO papers) and the quality of the profile spaces that create).

content.comment:
"The goal of EGTA is finding the NE of a game, which is also the goal of this paper."
I think this oversimplifies the paper's goal. PSRO with RRD isn't producing a strategy profile, it's returning a game. This is similar to my original comment about the paper: at least for me, the goal and problem domain are not clearly described. Stating that the goal is to find the NE of a game does not set the reader up for why they would care about exploration within an empirical game, how that might be evaluated, and interpreting the MRCP results.

Agree that simply using an approximate best response breaks the current version of Theorem 1. This needs to be fixed in some way, given the use of a sample-trained (approximate!) best-response oracle. An approximate version of the bound seems quite plausible.

Do the authors have any clarification about the magnitudes of the experimental results? My concern is that the regrets in both Leduc poker games seem rather large to be stopping with few iterations, and the few iterations used seems too short to see longer term behaviour in Leduc poker games or the random game of skill.

content.title: Reply to Discussion
content.comment:
As the reviewer states, PSRO with RRD returns an empirical game. However, the goal of PSRO is to construct an effective empirical game to capture the true NE and present that NE as a solution to the true game. So the ultimate goal is still to find the true NE.

The purpose of strategy exploration is to construct an effective game model with a minimal number of iterations (possibly due to the computational budget). With such purpose, we run a sufficient number of iterations (i.e., more than 100 iterations) in Leduc poker. After the selected number of iterations,  either there is a tiny improvement on the performance for all MSSs at each iteration or we exceed our assumption on limited computational budget. Moreover, our results are based on Openspiel and experiments can be easily reproduced and checked.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a new meta-strategy solver whose stopping criterion is based on regret criterion for the current empirical game. Embedded within the PSRO framework, it is then claimed that this procedure converges. The key idea behind this is that within the empirical game the profile space can contain strategies with lower regret than the target profile.

The authors then propose a method of tackling games with larger numbers of players for which current approaches are limited due to the explosive growth in required computation with the number of players. Specifically, the authors propose using a backward search method to avoid simulating the complete payoff matrix which is where the computational burden is normally occurred.

The ideas of the paper are supported by a range of experiments that demonstrate the beneficial characteristics of the approach.
content.main_review:
The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The explanation of the pressing issues are well-explained as is the rationale behind the proposed approach.   

From an intuitive perspective, the approach is well-justified, however little is done in the way of providing concrete theoretical results that prove better performance. Since, the contribution of the paper is mainly down to an introduction of two features, the overall contribution feels a little slight. The proof of the convergence guarantee is also very straightforward. Nevertheless, the paper is supported by decent empirical evaluations which give positive support for the ideas within the paper. 

As the authors state, some key ideas for the backward profile search technique were established in Brinkman & Wellman (2016). Elaborating more on why the adaptation of these ideas to the PSRO setting would be quite useful for evaluation the novelty of that part of the contribution.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper makes a useful contribution based which is justified by way of intuitive arguments and empirical evaluations. A drawback of the paper is that the extent of the contribution feels quite slight; including the theoretical contributions. This is magnified by the fact that the paper does not elaborate as to why the proposed BPS approach requires a meaningful degree of effort to adapt it to PSRO.

A positive aspect of the paper is that the ideas are supported by a range of encouraging empirical results.

content.title: Thanks for all the comments and suggestions.
content.comment: One key learning feature of PSRO is that newly added strategies are more likely to be in the support of a NE while the old ones would gradually disappear in the support. BPS is created based on this observation starting from new strategies in a game model and search towards old ones in contrast to the initial version of profile search in Brinkman & Wellman (2016). Since the newly added strategies are likely to be deviation strategies to previous equilibrium, following the old version would result in a situation where most of the profiles in the empirical game are evaluated. In a word, the key difference of BPS from the previous version is the incorporation of understanding of game learning with PSRO.
